explain: BERT uses only the Transformer encoder and looks at context in both directions; GPT uses only the decoder and is causal, T5 uses both (encoder-decoder).
options: Autoregressive decoder-only, generating one token at a time
Bidirectional encoder-only, reading the entire context
Text-to-text encoder-decoder, converting sequences
Convolutional network for images, without self-attention
q: Which Transformer architecture family does BERT belong to?

explain: GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) stacks only decoder blocks and predicts the next token; that is why it excels at text generation.
options: Autoregressive decoder-only, generating one token at a time
Bidirectional encoder-only, reading all the context together
Encoder-decoder with span corruption on inputs and outputs
Diffusion model that generates images from noise
q: Which Transformer architecture family does GPT belong to?

explain: T5 converts every problem (translation, summarization, classification, QA) into a text-in-text-out format, often with a prefix indicating the task.
options: It only predicts masked tokens with bidirectional context
It generates images from noise through a diffusion process
It frames every task as text-to-text conversion
It classifies input sentences without ever generating text
q: What characterizes the T5 text-to-text paradigm?

explain: A foundation model is pre-trained on huge generic corpora and then adapted to many downstream tasks via fine-tuning or prompting.
options: A small model trained from scratch for a single specific task
A linear regression model over hand-crafted features
A rigid model that cannot be adapted to new tasks
A model pre-trained on vast data and adaptable to many tasks
q: What is meant by foundation model?

explain: In masked language modeling a percentage of tokens is masked and the model predicts them using both left and right context.
options: Predicting the next token by looking only at past tokens
Predicting masked tokens using bidirectional context
Predicting whether the second sentence really follows the first in the text
Translating each sentence from the source to the target language
q: What does masked language modeling (MLM) as used by BERT consist of?

explain: Causal masking prevents the model from seeing future tokens, so next-token prediction depends only on previous ones.
options: The model cannot see future tokens during training
The model sees the whole sentence in both directions
The model randomly skips some layers during training
The model ignores the positional embeddings of the sequence
q: What does causal masking mean in models like GPT?

explain: Pre-training uses huge amounts of unlabeled text (expensive), while fine-tuning adapts the model to a specific task with labeled data (cheap).
options: They are two names for the same stage, with the same data and costs
Pre-training uses little labeled data, fine-tuning uses raw corpora
Pre-training on unlabeled text, task-specializing fine-tuning
Fine-tuning always comes before pre-training and defines its data and objective
q: What is the relationship between pre-training and fine-tuning?

explain: In zero-shot learning the prompt only describes the task, with no examples: the model must generalize thanks to what it learned in pre-training.
options: Giving the model hundreds of labeled examples in the prompt
Retraining all model weights from scratch on the new task
Showing the model a single demonstrative example of the task
Describing the task in the prompt without showing any example
q: What does zero-shot learning mean in prompting?

explain: BPE starts from characters and iteratively merges the most frequent symbol pairs until it reaches the desired vocabulary size.
options: By iteratively merging the most frequent symbol pairs
By choosing the merges that maximize estimated likelihood
By always splitting each word into isolated single characters
By using a fixed dictionary of predefined whole words
q: How does the Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) algorithm build its vocabulary?

explain: WordPiece, used by BERT, marks sub-tokens that continue a word with the ## prefix, so decoding knows where to rejoin the pieces.
options: The [MASK] symbol applied to obscured input tokens
The ## prefix on continuation sub-tokens
The Ġ symbol marked at the start of each new word
Curly braces around each word piece
q: Which convention does WordPiece use to mark sub-tokens inside a word?

explain: By splitting words into frequent sub-units, even a never-seen word can be represented as a sequence of known pieces: the OOV problem practically disappears.
options: By growing the vocabulary to millions of whole words
By converting every text into isolated single characters
By splitting rare words into known sub-units
By simply ignoring unknown words in the input
q: Why does subword tokenization solve the problem of never-seen-before words?

explain: Hallucination happens when the model produces fluent, plausible text that contains false or invented facts.
options: The generation of plausible but false text
A syntax error in model-generated code
Excessive overtraining on the original training set
Excessive slowness when generating responses
q: What is meant by hallucination in an LLM?

explain: Segment embeddings tell the model which sentence each token belongs to (sentence A or sentence B), information used in sentence-pair tasks.
options: The position of each token within the sequence
The lexical meaning of the single input word
Whether the input token is masked or not
Which of the two input sentences the token belongs to
q: What are segment embeddings for in BERT?

explain: In in-context learning the model performs the task by reading instructions and examples in the prompt, with no weight updates.
options: Fully retraining all weights on new data
Learning from examples in the prompt without touching the weights
Using a very high learning rate during training
Freezing the tokenizer before each new task
q: What is meant by in-context learning?

explain: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can process in a single input, prompt and examples included.
options: The total number of parameters learned in training
The number of Transformer layers stacked in the model
The maximum number of tokens processed in a single input
The total size of the tokenizer vocabulary
q: What is meant by the context window of an LLM?

explain: BERT is an autoencoder: it reconstructs corrupted inputs (masked tokens) with bidirectional context to understand; GPT is autoregressive: it predicts the future from the past to generate.
options: BERT reconstructs masked tokens, GPT predicts the next token
BERT generates text autoregressively and GPT classifies sentences into categories
Both only predict the next token by looking at previous tokens
Both use span corruption with special sentinel tokens
q: What is the difference between autoencoding models like BERT and autoregressive models like GPT?

explain: Being encoder-only and bidirectional, BERT produces excellent representations for classifying or extracting answers, but it is not designed to generate free text token after token.
options: Because it has too few parameters to generate fluent sentences
Because it does not use self-attention but only static word embeddings
Because its vocabulary is too small to generate text
Because it is encoder-only and non-causal, so it does not generate
q: Why is BERT not suited to free text generation?

explain: Autoregressive models show emergent capabilities with scale; generative and in-context reasoning tasks typically benefit from larger decoder-only models.
options: A small encoder-only model trained to classify
A large decoder-only model with few-shot prompting
A hand-written rule-based classifier built by experts
A tokenization-only model with no learned weights
q: What is the main advantage of large GPT models in few-shot learning?

explain: T5 uses a full encoder-decoder: the encoder reads the whole input and the decoder generates the output, an ideal structure for sequence-to-sequence transformations like summarization.
options: Because it is lighter than BERT and classifies without generating
Because it uses no attention but only local convolutions
Because it joins an input encoder and an output decoder
Because it requires no tokenization of the text
q: Why is an encoder-decoder model like T5 suited to abstractive summarization?

explain: Special tokens structure the input: [CLS] provides the aggregate representation for classification, [SEP] separates sentences, [MASK] marks tokens to predict.
options: [CLS] for the sequence, [SEP] between sentences, [MASK] on tokens
The three symbols have the same role and are interchangeable
They only serve to increase the vocabulary size
They are used only during text generation
q: What is the role of the special tokens [CLS], [SEP] and [MASK] in BERT?

explain: BPE merges the most frequent pairs, WordPiece merges those maximizing likelihood; both produce subword vocabularies but with different merge criteria.
options: BPE works at byte level, WordPiece at sentence level
There is no difference between the two merge algorithms
WordPiece is unable to handle rare words
BPE merges by frequency, WordPiece by likelihood
q: What is the main difference between BPE and WordPiece?

explain: Transfer learning reuses representations learned in pre-training: fine-tuning is its most common form for LLMs, with little labeled data and reduced cost.
options: Training a separate model from scratch for each task
Reusing pre-trained representations on new tasks
Automatic translation of texts from one language to another
Compressing the model for small, fast devices
q: What is meant by transfer learning in the context of LLMs?

explain: Positional embeddings inject token-order information, which self-attention alone would not perceive since it is permutation-invariant.
options: To reduce the total number of parameters to learn
To mask future tokens as in causal masking
To indicate the order of tokens in the sequence
To separate the two input sentences like segment embeddings
q: What are positional embeddings for in the Transformer?

explain: Next sentence prediction asked whether the second sentence really follows the first; later studies (e.g. RoBERTa) showed it is of little use and it is often removed.
options: Deciding whether the second sentence really follows the first
Predicting the next token of the sentence autoregressively
Translating the given sentence into another target language
Masking 15% of input tokens as in MLM
q: What was the goal of next sentence prediction (NSP) in BERT?

explain: Scaling laws describe predictable loss improvements as parameters, data and compute grow; beyond certain thresholds new capabilities emerge, such as in-context reasoning.
options: That small models always beat large ones
That vocabulary size never matters for performance
That training must always run on a single GPU
Predictable improvements with more parameters, data and compute
q: What do LLM scaling laws state?

explain: One-shot is an intermediate case: zero examples (zero-shot) versus a handful of examples (few-shot); with a single example it is called one-shot.
options: They are perfect synonyms meaning the same thing
One-shot shows a single example, few-shot shows several
One-shot requires full fine-tuning, few-shot only prompting
Few-shot updates the model weights, one-shot does not
q: What is the difference between one-shot and few-shot learning?

explain: In extractive QA, BERT predicts the start and end positions of the answer in the passage: it exploits bidirectional understanding without needing to generate text.
options: Extractive QA, classification and NER
Creative generation of original poems and stories
Generative machine translation between different languages
Speech synthesis with spoken audio generation
q: For which comprehension tasks is BERT particularly suited?

explain: SentencePiece treats the input as a raw Unicode sequence (spaces included) and needs no pre-tokenization: ideal for languages without spaces and multilingual vocabularies.
options: It always requires words already separated by whitespace
It does not handle Unicode characters of Asian languages
It works on raw text with spaces, without pre-tokenization
It works only with texts written in English
q: What is the advantage of SentencePiece over classic BPE and WordPiece?

explain: The model generates the statistically most plausible continuation, which may be false; checking sources and techniques like RAG reduce the risk.
options: By always raising the sampling temperature
Believing that a fluent output is always true
Using a smaller-than-needed vocabulary
Disabling text tokenization altogether
q: What is the most common trap related to hallucinations?

explain: With little labeled data it is better to leverage an already pre-trained model (fine-tuning or few-shot) instead of training from scratch, which would require huge corpora.
options: Training a Transformer from scratch on the few tickets
Fine-tuning a foundation model or few-shot
Hand-writing regular expressions for each category
Collecting billions of tokens before being able to start
q: A team has little labeled data for classifying support tickets. What is the best approach?

explain: Open-ended completion requires autoregressive generation: GPT is designed for this, while BERT (comprehension) and a T5 to adapt are worse choices for completing code on the fly.
options: An autoregressive decoder-only model like GPT
A bidirectional encoder-only model like BERT
A static parser based on grammar rules
An embeddings-only model with no decoder
q: Which model is best for code autocompletion in an IDE?

explain: Causal masking is only needed in autoregressive training/generation; for classifying with full context, the bidirectional masking of BERT is more suitable.
options: Using causal masking even inside a BERT model
Using a bidirectional encoder like BERT
Removing positional embeddings from the model
Tokenizing text at the level of whole unique sentences
q: To classify sentiment using all the context of the sentence, which choice is correct?

explain: Transfer from pre-training covers general grammar and facts; fine-tuning specializes style and task format with few targeted examples.
options: Pre-training is useless and learned weights should be discarded
Fine-tuning requires more data than the original pre-training
Weights learned in pre-training must always be reinitialized from scratch
Pre-training for the general base, fine-tuning to specialize it
q: Why does fine-tuning require much less data than pre-training?

explain: Subword tokenization depends on the tokenizer training corpus: rare specialist terms get fragmented into many pieces, lengthening sequences and worsening the representation.
options: The presence of the special tokens [CLS] and [SEP] in the input
The fragmentation of rare terms into too many sub-tokens
The use of causal masking blocking future context
The next sentence prediction objective in pre-training
q: What problem can a generic tokenizer cause when applied to highly specialized medical texts?

explain: T5 with task prefixes (e.g. a prefix indicating translation) handles translation, summarization and classification with the same generative interface.
options: Textual prefixes indicating the desired task
A separate model trained for each language
Complete removal of the encoder from the model
Total elimination of input tokenization
q: How does T5 indicate which task to perform on a given input?

explain: Extractive QA over documents requires locating exact spans in the text: bidirectional BERT excels here; a generator would risk paraphrasing or inventing references.
options: A pure text generator with no fidelity constraints
A diffusion model trained to generate images
A bidirectional encoder with span extraction heads
A retrieval system with no targeted reading of the text
q: A legal team must highlight the exact contract passages answering a question. Which architecture is best?

explain: Translation requires full reading of the source sentence (bidirectional encoder) plus fluent generation of the target (autoregressive decoder): the typical encoder-decoder profile.
options: A pure encoder-only with no generation at all
A decoder-only with no conditioning on the source
A single-sentence classifier with no generation
Encoder-decoder: full reading and generation
q: A team must translate technical manuals between two languages with high fidelity. Which architecture is most suitable and why?

explain: The distractor confuses BPE and WordPiece: BPE merges by raw pair frequency, WordPiece normalizes by the frequencies of the individual symbols (likelihood gain).
options: WordPiece merges the most frequent pairs, BPE maximizes likelihood
BPE merges by frequency, WordPiece by normalized likelihood
BPE uses the ## prefix, WordPiece uses the Ġ symbol instead
Both start from whole words rather than single characters
q: Which statement about BPE and WordPiece is correct?

explain: With a limited budget and document-grounded answers, RAG grounds the model in verifiable sources; massive fine-tuning on few documents risks overfitting and does not eliminate hallucinations.
options: Fully fine-tuning on thousands of internal documents
Raising the generation sampling temperature
Using retrieval-augmented generation over company documents
Training a new proprietary foundation model from scratch in-house
q: A startup on a small budget must answer questions about its own manuals without inventing content. Best strategy?

explain: Few-shot examples consume precious context and beyond a threshold gains diminish; longer prompts cost more and can introduce noise or position bias.
options: More examples always improve performance without limits
Few-shot examples take no context window space
Adding examples never changes the cost of each inference
Beyond a threshold benefits fade while costs and noise grow
q: What is the main limitation of few-shot learning with very many examples in the prompt?

explain: The causal model must never see the future during training: the triangular mask zeroes attention weights toward later positions.
options: A triangular mask hiding future tokens
No mask, with full bidirectional attention
A different random mask at each training step
Complete freezing of all decoder weights
q: How is causality implemented in the GPT self-attention mechanism?

explain: For NER, fine per-token contextual representations with left and right context are needed: the bidirectional BERT encoder with per-token classification is the standard choice.
options: Free text generation with a decoder-only model
Document retrieval only, with no targeted reading
A bidirectional encoder classifying each token
Translating records with an encoder-decoder
q: A hospital must recognize drug names and dosages in clinical records (NER). Which approach is most suitable?

explain: Emergence means qualitative new behavior beyond a scale threshold (e.g. in-context reasoning), not a simple linear fluency increase: that is why it is not guaranteed by doubling parameters.
options: A guaranteed linear increase in text fluency
New capabilities emerging beyond certain scale thresholds
Automatic reduction of hallucinations with scale
Total elimination of the need for training data
q: What does emergent capability mean in the context of scaling laws?

explain: With a single translated pair as example (one-shot) plus the instruction, a large decoder-only model can generalize the pattern without updating weights: a fast, cheap solution.
options: Training a dedicated neural translator from scratch
Pre-training a new multilingual foundation model
Fully fine-tuning on millions of parallel sentences
One-shot prompting with a large decoder-only model
q: An NGO must translate health notices into a low-resource language and has a single example sentence pair. Fastest solution?

explain: 15% is a trade-off: enough context to make the task challenging but enough signal to learn; much higher percentages would make reconstruction nearly impossible.
options: Because it is a random number chosen for no reason
Because it matches the vocabulary size used
To balance useful signal and task difficulty
Because the original dataset license requires it
q: Why does BERT mask about 15% of tokens in pre-training?

explain: Greedy decoding picks the highest-probability token at each step, with no sampling: it equals zero temperature and is the standard choice when reproducibility is needed.
options: The highest-probability token at each step
A token drawn at random from the whole available vocabulary
The rarest token to make the text more creative
Always the first token in alphabetical order in the text
q: In greedy decoding, which token is chosen at each generation step?

explain: Temperature reshapes the probability distribution before sampling: low values make it sharper and more deterministic, high values flatter and more creative.
options: The maximum number of tokens the model can generate as output
The randomness of the probability distribution
The size of the vocabulary used by the base model
The total length of the context window in use
q: What does the temperature parameter control in LLM generation?

explain: With top-p (nucleus sampling) only the nucleus of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p is considered: with p equal to 0.9, sampling happens within 90 percent of the probability mass.
options: Tokens with exactly 90% single probability
Only the single most probable token of all
The nucleus of tokens covering 90% of the mass
All tokens except the 90% most probable
q: With top-p equal to 0.9, from which set is the next token sampled?

explain: Top-k truncates the vocabulary to the k most probable tokens and samples only among them: with k equal to 1 it falls back to deterministic greedy decoding.
options: It generates exactly k complete alternative answers
It multiplies the probabilities of all tokens by k
It limits the vocabulary to special control tokens
It samples only among the k most probable tokens
q: What does the top-k parameter do during sampling?

explain: Beam search keeps multiple partial hypotheses in parallel and expands them at each step: with width 1 it matches greedy, with larger widths it explores more candidate sequences.
options: Multiple sequence hypotheses evaluated in parallel
A single token generated for the whole answer
Simultaneous translation into several different languages
Compressing the prompt into a few words
q: What does beam search maintain during generation compared to greedy decoding?

explain: Few-shot shows the model some examples of desired inputs and outputs inside the prompt: the model imitates the pattern without updating weights.
options: Retraining the weights on thousands of examples
Some examples of inputs and outputs inside the prompt
Completely disabling sampling
A vocabulary reduced to only known terms
q: What distinguishes a few-shot prompt from a zero-shot one?

explain: A stop sequence is a string that halts generation as soon as it is produced: it delimits the answer, for example stopping before inventing later dialogue turns.
options: The first word of the system prompt
The number of layers of the model used
The minimum temperature allowed in production
A string that stops generation
q: What is a stop sequence for in inference parameters?

explain: The max_tokens parameter caps the length of the generated answer: once the limit is reached, generation stops even mid-sentence.
options: The maximum length of the generated answer
The minimum size of the original training set
The number of languages supported by the base model
The number of GPUs used during training
q: What does the max_tokens parameter limit?

explain: The cited elements are the canonical prompt structure tested on the exam: a clear instruction, relevant context, input data, and an example or indicator of the expected output format.
options: Only the model name with its exact version
Instruction, context, input and output example
Only the temperature with the token limit
Only the list of internal weights of the model used
q: What are the key components of an effective prompt for an LLM?

explain: The root cause is statistical: the model predicts the most plausible continuation without grounding in facts, so it can confidently produce false but likely-sounding content.
options: Too much RAM on the local machine used
The lack of a dedicated graphics card for the task
Plausible predictions without grounding in facts
Using a low-resolution graphics monitor
q: What is the root cause of hallucinations in an LLM?

explain: Zero temperature equals greedy decoding: at each step the most probable token wins, so with the same prompt the output is deterministic and reproducible.
options: Much more creative and varied sampling in the text
An automatic increase of the total context window
An implicit translation of the text into English
The most deterministic and reproducible output
q: What happens when temperature is set to 0?

explain: Temperature warms the whole distribution (flattening or sharpening it), while top-p cuts off the tail of unlikely tokens before sampling: they act at two different points of the process.
options: Temperature reshapes the distribution, top-p filters tokens
Top-p changes the model weights while temperature freezes them
They are two different names for the same internal parameter
Temperature counts tokens and top-p counts total parameters
q: What is the difference between temperature and top-p?

explain: For factual, reproducible answers the deterministic setup is best: low temperature with restrictive top-p, keeping the model anchored to the most probable tokens.
options: High temperature with very broad top-p
Low temperature with restrictive top-p
Maximum temperature with unlimited top-k
Random sampling with no filter at all
q: Which setup is best for a factual question-answering system in production?

explain: Beam search maximizes the overall sequence probability but can produce repetitive, generic texts; sampling with temperature adds variety at the cost of less control over average quality.
options: Beam search is always faster than greedy decoding
Sampling never uses the token probabilities estimated by the model
Beam search explores the probable, sampling adds variety
Greedy decoding generates more creative texts than free sampling
q: What is the trade-off between beam search and stochastic sampling?

explain: Pre-training teaches general knowledge over huge unlabeled corpora, while instruction tuning refines the model to follow instructions with curated instruction-response pairs.
options: Fully fine-tuning all weights of the base model used
Training the model from scratch on a single new task
General pre-training and refinement on instruction-response pairs
Compressing the model for modern mobile devices
q: What is the difference between pre-training and instruction tuning?

explain: Tokenization happens before the model and affects costs and truncations: the same text yields a different token count with different tokenizers, consuming more or less context window.
options: The color of charts inside the technical documentation
The speed of the GPU fan used in the server
The time zone of the remote inference server used
Cost, latency and context window usage
q: Why does tokenization affect inference cost and latency?

explain: The model estimates about four characters per token in English: a word like the one cited therefore splits into several subword tokens instead of taking just one.
options: Into several subword tokens, about one every four characters
Always into a single token per whole word
Into one token per each capital letter used
Into zero tokens because long words are always skipped
q: In English a token covers about four characters: into how many tokens does a rare word like "antidisestablishmentarianism" split?

explain: Beam search with width k keeps the k partial hypotheses with the highest cumulative score: it broadens exploration versus greedy but remains a deterministic search, with no random sampling.
options: It samples k random tokens at each single generation step
It ignores probabilities and picks hypotheses fully at random
It keeps the k partial hypotheses with the highest score
It generates k independent answers with different random seeds
q: How does beam search with width (beam width) equal to k work?
source: Adattata da Udemy – sample gratuito NCA-GENL

explain: Dynamic nucleus sampling adapts the nucleus at each step: with peaked distributions few tokens suffice, with flat ones the nucleus widens, unlike top-k which always truncates to the same fixed number.
options: Top-k is dynamic while top-p always stays fixed
They are identical and interchangeable in every single use case
Top-p fully ignores the probabilities of candidate tokens
Top-p adapts the nucleus, top-k truncates to a fixed number
q: Why is top-p called dynamic sampling compared to top-k?

explain: High temperature flattens the distribution and gives weight even to the unlikely tail: on factual tasks this directly raises the chance of generating false but fluent content.
options: High temperature on factual questions without verification
Zero temperature on a standard classification task
Top-k equal to 1 on code snippets to complete
A short stop sequence on particularly long answers
q: Which sampling choice most increases the risk of hallucinations?

explain: The penalty lowers the score of already generated tokens and pushes the model toward new alternatives: it counters the repetitive loops typical of greedy decoding on long texts.
options: Raising the temperature to the highest possible value today
Penalizing already generated tokens to favor novelty
Fully disabling the stop sequence used in output
Doubling the model vocabulary size
q: A model in greedy decoding repeats the same sentence in a loop. Which intervention is most targeted?

explain: The end-of-turn delimiter stops the model from continuing past the planned point: without a stop sequence the model would keep generating, inventing later turns of the conversation.
options: A stop sequence on the end-of-turn delimiter
A very high temperature to vary the style used
An unlimited top-k over the whole model vocabulary
A max_tokens equal to the whole context window used
q: A chatbot keeps generating the user's later turns by itself. Which fix is most direct?

explain: Silent truncation cuts the prompt or answer when the budget is exceeded: counting tokens before sending and reserving room for the output avoids losing instructions or clipped endings.
options: Ignoring the limit and sending everything anyway
Counting tokens and reserving budget for the output
Raising the temperature to compress the text
Changing the prompt language on each request
q: A long prompt plus the answer exceeds the context window. What is the correct mitigation?

explain: Self-consistency samples several independent reasoning chains and votes on the final answer: agreement across different paths signals the most robust conclusions on logic problems.
options: Translating the prompt into three different languages
Retraining on three different datasets
Majority vote over several reasoning chains
The arithmetic mean of the weights of three distinct models
q: What does the self-consistency technique applied to Chain-of-Thought consist of?
source: Adattata da Udemy – sample gratuito NCA-GENL

explain: Evaluation with step decomposition allows locating the error: the model may get an intermediate step wrong while guessing the result, and only inspecting the chain reveals it.
options: The number of parameters of the model used in the test
The generation speed in tokens per second measured
The dollar cost of each single model call
The correctness of the steps, not just the result
q: How do you evaluate whether a Chain-of-Thought is truly solid?

explain: Specifying the format with an example guides the model toward parseable outputs: it reduces ambiguity and makes downstream automatic processing reliable.
options: Always leaving the format fully free and implicit
Showing an example of the desired output format
Asking for answers as long as possible every time
Forbidding any example inside the submitted prompt
q: Why is it worth specifying the output format in the prompt?

explain: One-shot is the intermediate case between zero examples and few examples: a single example is enough to show the expected format and style without taking too much context.
options: A prompt with a single demonstrative example
A prompt with no explicit written instruction
A model trained on a single initial token
A tokenizer with a single symbol in the vocabulary
q: What does one-shot learning mean in prompting?
